en: An Introductory Discourse on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Clarified by Guanheng.
Composed for the *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa-tathāgataguhyahetu-bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā-nītārtha-sarvabodhisattva-daśasāhasra-śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
The three characters "Dafo ding" (Great Buddha-Crown) are used here as the name for the Dharma; they manifest the title of the most supreme and unsurpassed honor of the Dharma.
To speak of the "Great Buddha-Crown" refers to the *uṣṇīṣa*—the cranial protuberance—which is the most exalted and peerless among the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata.
Indeed, the Tathāgata’s entire being transcends both the mundane and supramundane realms; even his mark of the wheels on the soles of his feet is likewise transcendent.
Because he transcends both the mundane and the supramundane, the holy ones and ordinary beings of the nine realms all prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.

Since the Buddha’s feet are already most supreme and exalted, one can know that among the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, the wheels on his soles are at the very bottom, while the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance) is at the very top.
This mark of the crown is the supreme mark within the Buddha’s entire, unsurpassed body. Observe, for instance, those within the triple world:
Regarding external phenomena, both sentient and insentient, this is the subtle and wondrous realm of the sages and ordinary beings. Where else could there be anything more venerable than this place?
Where else could there be anything more sublime than this place? Not only is there nothing more venerable or more sublime;

within the subtle and wondrous forms and appearances of the sages and ordinary beings, there is certainly not a single dharma that can equal this place. Is it not the case that this appearance is the unsurpassed among the unsurpassed?
Yes. At this place, the Tathāgata emitted light and spoke mantras to certify the Dharma; thus, at this unsurpassed site, he revealed the reality of the unsurpassed Dharma.

Initially, the Tathāgata himself designated its name: there is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the myriad practices and is the wondrously adorned path by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend through a single gate.

These three phrases concerning "the path of wondrous adornment that transcends through a single gate" of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions were spoken because Ānanda had requested the initial expedient means for the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to attain the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* of Bodhi;
thus, the Tathāgata responded to his request by means of this "path of wondrous adornment that transcends through a single gate" of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
This is the explicit teaching of the Unsurpassed by means of the name "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
At the end of the eighth fascicle, the title is further established as: *The Sūtra Named the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Sitātapatrā-Anuttara-Ratnamudrā*.
This is the implicit teaching of the Unsurpassed by means of the name "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. Thus, it is known that this sūtra is designated as such in both its explicit and implicit aspects.
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. At the very beginning, when the Tathāgata was invited into the royal palace, he knew that Ānanda had been afflicted by sorcery.
Having finished his meal and returned, the Tathāgata then emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness.
From within this light, a thousand-petaled jeweled lotus emerged, upon which a transformation Buddha sat in the full-lotus posture and proclaimed a divine mantra, commanding Mañjuśrī.
Beneficial. I shall go to protect you with this mantra. This Tathāgata first spoke this unsurpassed mantra at this unsurpassed place.
Within the seventh fascicle, at the request of Ānanda, he proclaimed it again. At that time, from within his *uṣṇīṣa*, the World-Honored One emitted a hundred jewel-lights;
from within these lights emerged thousand-petaled jewel lotuses, upon which transformation-Tathāgatas sat amidst the jeweled flowers, emitting light from their crowns.

There were ten paths of light from a hundred jewels; each and every ray of light universally manifested ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* numbers of Vajrapāṇis, who held mountains and wielded clubs, pervading the realm of empty space.

The great assembly gazed upward, feeling both awe and affection, and sought the Buddha’s compassionate protection as they listened with single-minded devotion to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Emitting Light from the Inconceivable Crown, as he proclaimed this divine mantra. This is as follows:

In the second instance, he was at the Unsurpassed Place (*anuttara-pada*), where he emitted light and proclaimed the Unsurpassed Mantra. This esoteric teaching is named the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa (*mahā-buddhoṣṇīṣa*).
Because these two instances occurred while he was at this Unseen-Uṣṇīṣa (*adṛśya-uṣṇīṣa*) emitting light and proclaiming the mantra, this constitutes the factual basis for its name.
The five-fascicle version states: "At that moment, the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions shook in six ways, like motes of dust..."
Those who have come to dwell in this world each possess a precious light that issues from their crowns.
At the same moment, these lights arrive at the Jeta Grove in that world and drench the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.

This Tathāgata, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions, first emits light from the Unsurpassed Place to perform the rite of mutual drenching, thereby realizing this unsurpassed Śūraṅgama Dharma. As it says in the sixth fascicle: "Thus..."

At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One simultaneously emitted jewel-like radiance, which reached far to moisten the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, as well as the various Bodhisattvas who are Dharma Princes.
Those Tathāgatas likewise simultaneously emitted jewel-like radiance from their five limbs;
from the directions as numerous as motes of dust, this light came to moisten the crown of the Buddha’s head, as well as the crowns of the great Bodhisattvas in the assembly.
Arhat. This is the second instance in which this Tathāgata, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions, receives the mutual empowerment of intersecting lights from the Unsurpassed State.
This reveals the unsurpassed Śūraṅgama Dharma; its explicit teaching is called the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.

Because of these two instances of empowerment through intersecting lights, it is said that there is actual realization. Furthermore, the recitation of the mantra from the light upon the crown is esoteric, while also being exoteric.
The mutual interpenetration of light and the conferral of empowerment manifest both the Exoteric and the Esoteric, which are harmoniously integrated with one another.

It is also named "The Mass of Light from the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa" and also named "The Tathāgata’s Uṣṇīṣa. These fourfold designations correspond to the fourfold emissions of light; thus, [the title] consists of the three characters "Great Buddha-uṣṇīṣa."
Therefore, by abiding in renown, one uses renown to manifest the Dharma; thus, the title of "the Ultimate, Unsurpassed Mystery" is clearly established.
As for "the secret cause of the Tathāgata," this uses the person to manifest the Dharma. The Tathāgata is the person of fruition; in relation to this Śūraṅgama Dharma, he is its secret cause.
Furthermore, this cites the unsurpassed person to manifest the unsurpassed Dharma. This Dharma is subtle and wondrous.
It is called "Mystery" (Mi) because it is unsurpassed; it is called "Cause" (In) because the Tathāgata attains the fruit by relying upon it;

thus, it is termed the "Mysterious Cause. "Tathāgata" is one of the ten titles of the Buddhas. "Tathā" (Thus) refers to the Name according to Principle, while "Gata" (Come) refers to the Title according to Wisdom.

Because Wisdom and Principle are conjoined, and stillness and illumination are non-dual, he is named Tathāgata. Although sentient beings possess the principle of the original awakening of suchness (tathatā), yet...

The wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-jñāna*) has no place to return; yet, it mistakenly perceives the fundamental essence—which is suchness (*tathatā*) and immovable—as the deluded appearances of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

For this reason, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). The Tathāgata, relying on the principle of suchness, emptiness, and quiescence, gives rise to the vast and all-pervading wisdom that illuminates and shatters all worldly and transworldly phenomena, realizing that they are entirely empty in their very substance, such that not a single dharma exists.

Because there is no obstruction, wisdom merges with principle; because essence and function are one and the same, it receives this name. Furthermore, the word "like" (ru) signifies that sentient beings and Buddhas share the same name, the "True Cause" (zhengyin).
The Tathāgata relies upon this to realize the fruit, which is called the "Secret Cause" (miyin).

This secret cause of the Tathāgata has no other cause; it is precisely the essence of suchness itself. As the Sūtra says: "If, at the stage of the causal ground, one uses [a mind of] arising and ceasing..."
To take the mind as the fundamental cause for cultivation and seek the Buddha-vehicle—which is neither born nor extinguished—is impossible. Furthermore, it says:

"If you now wish to cause seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, you should first select the root of birth and death, rely upon the nature that is neither born nor extinguished and is perfectly profound and tranquil, and by means of this tranquility, revolve against its false appearances to extinguish birth and death. Again...
The awakening that returns to the source: one attains the nature of the primordial, luminous, and non-arising wisdom, which serves as the fundamental cause for cultivation.

Thereafter, one perfectly achieves the realization of the stage of fruition. Thus, the Tathāgata takes "suchness" (tathatā) as the cause; this is called the secret cause. Taking "suchness" as the fruit; this is the wondrous fruit.
Since both cause and fruit are the single essence of suchness, they are the identity of cause and fruit. [This concludes the character] "Lai" (come).

Illuminating the essence of suchness as fundamentally empty is called the wisdom of suchness-as-reason (*tathatā-jñāna*). Illuminating the essence of suchness as being both existent and such is the wisdom of suchness-as-phenomenon (*tathatā-vastu-jñāna*).

Illuminating the essence of suchness as neither empty nor existent, yet both empty and existent, is called the all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). This wisdom arises from principle (*li*), while principle is manifested through wisdom.
There is no wisdom apart from suchness, and no suchness apart from wisdom; thus, reason and wisdom are one and the same. This is the relationship between cause and effect.
The principle of wisdom relies on the person to explain the secret cause; that is, the dharma which serves as the cause. It possesses the three truths and the three contemplations:

relying on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one gives rise to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), and this empty contemplation illuminates the ultimate truth; relying on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one gives rise to the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), and this provisional contemplation illuminates the conventional truth;

relying on the middle-way truth (*madhyamā-pratipad-satya*), one gives rise to the contemplation of the middle way (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*), and this middle contemplation illuminates the middle truth. These three truths are precisely suchness (*tathatā*), immovable.

*Li* (Principle). The three contemplations (*sanguan*) are precisely the wisdom of universal illumination (*bianzhao-zhi*) mentioned above. In terms of that which practices and realizes, they are the person (*ren*);

in terms of that which is practiced and realized, they are the Dharma (*fa*). As indicated by the three truths (*sandi*) following the character *ru* (Suchness), the character *lai* (Come) is named from these three contemplations.

Thus, the Tathāgata takes the three contemplations and the three truths as the secret cause (*miyin*). The three contemplations collectively form the single character *lai*, and the three truths collectively...
This reveals the single character "As" (如). That which comes is not external to "As. This, moreover, is the single suchness of person and dharmas.
Thus, it is clear that person, dharma, cause, effect, wisdom, and principle are all the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
"Cultivation and realization of the definitive meaning" (xiūzhèng liǎoyì) precisely clarifies that cause and effect, person and phenomena, and subject and object are identical and without remainder.

To cultivate in accordance with suchness is cultivation of the definitive meaning; there is nothing else to be cultivated. To realize in accordance with suchness is realization of the definitive meaning;

there is nothing else to be realized. Therefore, it is called "cultivation and realization of the definitive meaning. These two characters, "cultivation" (xiū) and "realization" (zhèng), apply universally to person and phenomena, wisdom and principle, and cause and effect.
As for the fruit: that which is capable of being cultivated and realized is termed the person and wisdom; that which is cultivated and realized is termed the dharma and principle.
Cultivation is the cause; realization is the fruit. Thus, it is clearly understood that the person, dharma, principle, wisdom, cause, and fruit are all one and the same.
Regarding "the myriad practices of all bodhisattvas": "bodhisattva" refers to the practitioner capable of cultivation; "myriad practices" refers to the dharmas being cultivated.

To say "the Tathāgata above" refers to the awakening of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*); this clarifies the cause through the fruition, revealing that the essence of this Śūraṅgama Samādhi—suchness and immovability—is the secret cause.
"Bodhisattva" is the mind of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*); this clarifies the practice of the cause through the revelation of this Śūraṅgama [Samādhi].
The essence of the *Śūraṅgama*—the suchness that is immovable—is fully endowed with the myriad practices. These myriad practices and the secret cause are, in their totality, one identical essence.
Taken collectively, they are called the "secret cause"; taken individually, they are called the "myriad practices. There is no separate essence or separate meaning between them.
Śūraṅgama is the collective name for the secret cause of the three contemplations and the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas. In the Sanskrit language it is called Śūraṅgama;
here it is translated as "Ultimate Solidity. This is because Buddhas and sentient beings share the same body of suchness—unmoving and solid.

Fundamentally, there are no distinctions of names and characteristics such as saint and ordinary being, delusion and awakening, birth and death, or coming and going. Sentient beings simply fail to realize this.

One falsely perceives various marks of differentiation—such as the noble and the ordinary, delusion and enlightenment, going and coming, birth and death, internal and external, small and large, existence and non-existence.
This is to perceive the immovable and solid essence as having the marks of birth, death, coming, going, and decay. It is due to this inverted and erroneous clinging.
They generate suffering and affliction for themselves, sinking deeper and deeper, becoming more deluded and more immersed; how can they alone be helped?
Out of compassion for them, the Tathāgata reveals the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma, enabling them to ultimately investigate all phenomena:

what is born and what ceases, where does one go and from where does one come? Ultimately, one reaches the point of not seeing a single dharma being born, not seeing a single dharma ceasing, and not seeing anything [existing].
In reality, as phenomena depart, no phenomenon is seen to go; in reality, as phenomena arrive, no phenomenon is seen to come.
One thus perceives the original face of all phenomena, which is none other than the immovable and steadfast fundamental essence of one's own house. Therefore, it is called "ultimately steadfast.
This single title of the sutra is fully exhausted by these two characters, "steadfast. This steadfastness is the body of suchness, immovable, and eternally abiding truth.

The mind. This resolute mind is ever-quiescent while illuminating; this is called principle (*li*) and phenomena (*fa*). It is ever-illuminating while quiescent; this is called wisdom (*zhi*) and person (*ren*).

To cultivate based upon this quiescence and illumination is called cultivation of the definitive meaning (*liao-yi*). To realize in accord with this quiescence and illumination is called realization of the definitive meaning.

Taken as a whole, it is called the secret cause; divided, it is called the myriad practices (*wan-xing*). Thus, these are the world of person and phenomenon, wisdom and principle, cause and effect, cultivation and realization.
The sentient and insentient of the supramundane are, in total, the one firm and wondrous mind. By means of this firmness, one seeks out the myriad dharmas;
yet what myriad dharmas could there be? By means of the myriad dharmas, one investigates this firmness; the firmness becomes manifest. Is this not the ultimate, firm, and great liberation?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata himself established five names for this sutra, which the compiler has here summarized.
The essentials of these five names are all encompassed within this single title. The first name is: *Mahā-buddhoṣṇīṣa-sitātapatrā-anuttara-ratnamudrā-daśadig-tathāgata-viśuddha-samudranetra*.
Among these, the ten characters from *sitātapatrā* to *anuttara-ratnamudrā* explain the esoteric (mantra) aspect and do not encompass the exoteric;
therefore, they are not included here. The eight characters from *daśadig-tathāgata* onward explain... [the exoteric].
The three characters "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Mahā-uṣṇīṣa*) elucidate both the Exoteric and Esoteric; therefore, they are adopted.
Subsequently, the explanation of the mantra from the "Light on the Crown" elucidates the Esoteric meaning, while the "Consecration by the Intertwining Light" elucidates the Exoteric meaning.
The second [section] is titled "Saving and Protecting One's Kinsmen, Delivering Ānanda and the Matangi Woman, Attaining the Bodhicitta, and Entering the Ocean of Universal Knowledge."

In this context, the phrase "the cause for the protection of kinsmen" extends only as far as Mātanga; it designates the person who initiates the teaching but does not encompass the teaching initiated.
The eight characters beginning with "attaining the bodhicitta" designate only the resultant dharmas and do not pervade the causal dharmas; therefore, they are not included.
The third name is *Mahāvaipulya-saddharmapuṇḍarīka-rāja-daśadig-buddha-mātṛkā-dhāraṇī-mantra*. Within this, the word "Great" (Mahā) [is explained as follows]:...

The seven characters "fangguǎng děng" (方廣等) encompass the exoteric teachings but do not express the esoteric; furthermore, because the character "dà" (大) in "Dàfāngguǎng zhòngdà fódǐng" (大方廣重大佛頂) is already present, these are not selected.
The eight characters "shífāng fó mǔ děng" (十方佛母等) express the esoteric but do not encompass the exoteric;
furthermore, because the character "fó" (佛) in "Shífāng fó mǔ zhòngdà fódǐng" (十方佛母重大佛頂) is already present, these are also not selected. The fourth name is "Rúlái mìyīn xiū" (如來密因修).
"Realizing the definitive meaning. These eight characters encompass both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings; therefore, they are taken in their entirety.

At the very beginning, the Tathāgata first proclaims that the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama King is fully endowed with the myriad practices and is the single path through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend to the wondrously adorned way.
This is manifest as the secret cause of the Tathāgatas. Later, in the seventh fascicle, it says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by means of this..."
By means of this mantra, one attains the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This secret is the esoteric cause of the Tathāgatas. As the Sūtra says:
"These various stages are all entered through the diamond-like observation of the ten profound metaphors;
within *śamatha*, one employs the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas to purify, cultivate, and realize them, thereby gradually gaining entry. This reveals the full cultivation, realization, and mastery.

Regarding the meaning: the Sūtra states that even if one does not personally perform meritorious deeds oneself, all the merits of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall be bestowed upon this person.
By virtue of this, for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—indeed, unspeakably unspeakable kalpas—one shall always be born in the same place as the Buddhas.
Immeasurable merits, like clusters of akṣa fruits, will be cultivated together in that same location.

"Forever without dispersal. This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) fully realized through the Secret [Mantra]. Furthermore, it says: "Such accumulated karma will vanish like snow melting in hot water;
before long, all shall attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Again, it says:

"If these sons of good family do not attain mental mastery within this very body born of their parents, then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods. This is the definitive meaning fully realized through the Secret [Mantra].
Furthermore, that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmitted this *dhāraṇī-hṛdaya* because of it constitutes the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

From Ānanda, if it were said that in all worlds, according to whatever lands they may be, for all sentient beings born in those lands, [the teachings] would be written on birch bark, palm leaves, and so forth, reaching the Tathāgatas of the ten directions—this would be a falsehood.
This merely pertains to the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) of practice; it is esoteric.

It possesses the authentic evidence for the cultivation and realization of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). This cultivation and realization of the definitive meaning clearly elucidates both the exoteric and esoteric senses.
The fifth is titled "The Chapter on Empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), the *Śūraṃgama* of the Ten Thousand Practices of All Bodhisattvas.

As for this "Chapter on Empowerment," it mostly belongs to the Esoteric division (*guhyatantra*). Even if it were to include exoteric elements, it is nonetheless significant; furthermore, because it emphasizes the word "Crown" (*uṣṇīṣa*) from "Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-śīrṣa," I have not selected it. For example:

In this sutra, the three gradual stages, the chapter on the Perfect Penetration of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, the attainment of the two excellences and the four inconceivables, and the explicit exposition of the myriad practices of the bodhisattvas are presented.
At the end of the seventh fascicle, it says: "Therefore, it can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify their roots of discipline;
it causes those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them; and it causes those who have not yet practiced with diligence to attain [it]."
Vigor: it causes those without wisdom to attain wisdom; it causes those who are not pure to quickly attain purity;

it causes those who do not observe the fasts and precepts to spontaneously fulfill them, and so forth. This is the secret endowment of the ten thousand practices of bodhisattvas; these are the ten thousand practices of all bodhisattvas.
This title expresses both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings. *Śūraṃgama* is the general name for the great samādhis of both the Exoteric and Esoteric traditions; therefore, it is taken from both.
Thus, this title is formed by taking portions from the first and second [sections] and the entirety of the fourth.

The word "sūtra" (經) refers to the teaching that expresses [the meaning]; in Sanskrit it is *sūtra*, which here is translated as "Scripture of Accordance" (*kīng-kyǒng*). This means it accords with principle and accords with...
The Master’s words: because it briefly accords with the written characters, it is simply called a "sūtra. This refers to the text and phrases of the ten fascicles;

the aforementioned nineteen characters represent the meaning expounded within those ten fascicles. Since the text and its meaning are combined as a single name, it is titled *The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
The text and meaning of these ten fascicles of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* do not exceed the meaning of the nine phrases requested by Ānanda.
Ānanda regretted that his own cultivation of the power of the Hīnayāna path was incomplete, such that he could not subdue the *Sāvitra* spell.
He wished to request the supreme cause of the wondrous Bodhi—the complete and perfect power of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions—hoping that the Buddha would illuminate it for him.
This is the cause of Bodhi; by relying upon it for cultivation and realization, one achieves the wondrous fruit of Bodhi.
Having fully perfected the power of the Buddha-way, one immediately attains great sovereignty. Such is the intent behind Ānanda’s request.
The Tathāgata, about to reveal the wondrous cause of Bodhi, first waited for Ānanda to manifest the depth and shallowness of his ailment;

only then would he prescribe the wondrous remedy according to the disease. When the medicine and the symptoms corresponded, both the true and the false were simultaneously dispelled, and he immediately returned to his original countenance and accomplished the body of wisdom, becoming equal to the Buddha in the power of the Great Way. Thus did the World-Honored One diagnose Ānanda’s illness.

At the initial stage of generating the bodhicitta, there is inversion: perceiving the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) is the deluded object; the seeing that perceives them is the deluded faculty;

and the mind that feels attachment is the deluded consciousness. Since these three—faculty, object, and consciousness—are all delusive, one becomes confused regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, unable to penetrate the pure true reality (*dharmatā*).
The Tathāgata, by means of the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama, possesses the three sublime contemplations.
This is the ultimate refinement. Each [delusion] is successively dismantled until one reaches the pure, true reality—the firm and immovable essence—and only then does it cease.
First, one dismantles the deluded mind of attachment; this deluded mind belongs to the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The Tathāgata first employs *śamatha* to demonstrate that the nature of pervasive conceptualization is ultimately without substance, thereby revealing the firm, fundamental *tathāgatagarbha* as emptiness.

The Body. From the first fascicle, beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, extended his golden arm and stroked Ānanda’s crown, informing Ānanda and the great assembly that there is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King," up until the second fascicle, where it says:
"The four meanings are accomplished; you should know this hereafter: when the seeing sees, that seeing is not [the object]."

"If even the seeing of seeing is already removed from seeing and cannot be reached by it, how can you further speak of causes and conditions, spontaneity, and the characteristics of their conjunction?
You śrāvakas are narrow-minded, inferior, and lacking in knowledge; you are unable to penetrate the pure, true reality (*dharmatā*). I now instruct you:
contemplate this well and do not become weary on the wondrous path to Bodhi. This passage serves to refute the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The *Manifestation of the Tathāgatagarbha* elucidates the meaning of *śamatha*, which is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Within this, the initial section refutes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), beginning from the "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations" up to the second fascicle, where the Buddha reprimands Ānanda, saying:
"You and others are people who are doubly deluded; you are no different from my hanging down a hand," and so forth, describing them as objects of the Tathāgata’s compassion.
This is the cessation. This is the section on the subsequent refutation of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
It begins from "Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, wept and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:

'Although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha and awakened to the wondrously luminous mind, which is fundamentally the perfectly complete and eternally abiding ground of the heart,' and continues until the end: 'I shall not grow weary or indolent upon the path to wondrous Bodhi. This is it."

From the second fascicle: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has for our sakes expounded upon the characteristics of causal conditions and spontaneity, as well as those of conjunction and non-conjunction, my mind remains unenlightened.

Now, having further heard and seen [the teaching on] 'seeing seeing' and 'not-seeing,' my confusion and distress increase all the more. I prostrate myself in hope that your vast compassion will bestow the eye of great wisdom and open [my understanding]."
"Reveal to us the clarity and purity of the awakened mind. Having spoken these words, they prostrated with tears of compassion and received the holy instruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of pity for Ānanda and the great assembly, was about to expound the path of wondrous cultivation for the various *samādhis* of the Great *Dhāraṇī*.
[This occurs] up to the third fascicle; therefore, one should know that mental phenomena (*dharmas*) serve as conditions.

Since the consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) is entirely absent in these three locations, the mind, mental objects, and the mind-element—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature;
they simply cease. This passage generally refutes the nature of causal conditions to reveal the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* and clarify the meaning of *samādhi*;
this is the provisional contemplation (*jia guan*). Within it, the text first clarifies two kinds of deluded views to demonstrate the basis of causal conditions.
He first refutes Ānanda’s view that seeing the Buddha is a false vision. Next, he integrates the four aggregates into reality.

He then specifically refutes the nature of causes and conditions, thereby refuting the reason why Ānanda considers the Buddha’s marks and signs to be false appearances. In summary, he refutes it by saying:
"You still do not understand that all these superficial, illusory, and transformative phenomena arise from their very place and perish as they are encountered; they are illusory and false."
Regarding their characteristics: their nature is truly the essence of wondrously enlightened clarity.

Thus, from the five aggregates and six sense bases, through the twelve entrances up to the eighteen realms, they arise falsely through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and they are falsely said to perish when causes and conditions separate.
Yet they are utterly incapable of knowing that arising and ceasing, going and coming, are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha—eternally abiding, wondrously clear, and immovable.

The wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is all-pervasive and circular. Within this true and eternal nature, if one seeks for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death, nothing at all can be found.
Thus we know that the Buddha’s marks and signs, as well as bodhi, do not transcend what is subsumed within the five aggregates and the other four categories.

There is only the distinction between that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*), as well as the distinction from sentient beings. From the third fascicle, Ānanda said to the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has constantly taught that all the various transformations in the world arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, manifesting due to the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
How is it that the Tathāgata now rejects both causes and conditions and spontaneity (*svabhāva*)? I am now..."

Not knowing to which category this meaning belongs, I pray you will compassionately grant us an exposition for the sake of all sentient beings: the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation.
[It continues: "Later on, you will fundamentally not realize that within the Tathāgata-garbha, the nature-consciousness is luminous awareness, the true consciousness of awakened clarity;
this wondrous awakening is profoundly still and pervades the entire Dharma-realm, encompassing and exhaling the ten voids—how could it have a fixed location? It arises according to karma."
The appearance of the world, with ignorance and delusion as its causes and conditions, and its inherent nature—all these are merely the conceptual calculations of the discerning mind;

they exist only as verbal expressions and possess no real meaning. This [passage] demonstrates the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), revealing the Tathāgatagarbha as both empty and non-empty, and elucidating the meaning of *dhyāna*.
This is precisely the Middle Way contemplation. Within it, that which is pure and fundamental is emptiness.

Phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*). Their manifestation according to karma is the provisional aspect (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*). Emptiness does not obstruct the provisional manifestation according to karma; the provisional does not obstruct emptiness, being inherently pure and fundamental.
This is the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), also called the Middle Way of Definitive Meaning (*nītārtha*).

Because Ānanda has mastered the characteristics of the three contemplations and awakened to the perfect, eternally abiding True Mind, he speaks a verse to praise the Buddha and makes a vow for the benefit [of others].

Born [into this world], he seeks to repay the Buddha’s kindness. Previously, when elucidating the essence and characteristics of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), he merely clarified the seven characters of *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*;
he had not yet explained that the perfect subtlety of the three contemplations is fundamentally one mind. From the beginning of the fourth fascicle:
"At that time, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, being in the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder..."
Placing his right shoulder and right knee upon the ground, he joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, you have skillfully expounded for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*). From the beginning up to the fourth fascicle, [the text describes how] some may transcend their fetters or receive predictions of enlightenment.
Why do you still allow us to remain as listeners and observers? You deceive yourself! This passage clarifies and resolves doubts regarding the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

The subtlety of the three contemplations elucidates the subtle character of "subtle *śamatha*. Within this, the initial explanation resolves doubts regarding the three contemplations and reveals the subtlety of their intrinsic characteristics.
Next, it perfectly integrates them within the one mind, revealing the subtlety of their perfect fusion, perfect awakening, and perfect cultivation.
This as a whole elucidates the subtle character of "subtle *śamatha*"; the above has thus revealed "subtle *śamatha*."
The eight characters of *śamatha-samādhi-dhyāna* are clear and manifest. These eight characters consist solely of the two words "mysterious cause" (*mi-yin*).

"Mysterious" (*miao*) is precisely "mystery" (*mi*); *śamatha* and the others are the "cause. From the fourth fascicle, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instructions, had their doubts eliminated;
they awakened to the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), and their bodies and minds attained ease and tranquility, experiencing something unprecedented. They rose from their seats.

In the seventh fascicle, the World-Honored One states: "If an evil Māra or his retinue should come to harass this good person, I shall shatter their heads with my precious vajra-pestle until they are like fine dust, and I shall forever cause the endeavors of this person to be fulfilled as desired.
This clarifies the four characters of the "Initial Expedient Means" (*ādikarmika-upāya*). Within this, the first part elucidates the arising of the two definitive meanings.
In the sixth fascicle, Ānanda and the great assembly attained clear understanding in both body and mind, receiving a profound revelation.
They perceived the Buddha’s Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa as being like a person who has traveled far on business and, before returning home, clearly understands the path leading back to their own house.
Thus, immeasurable sentient beings all gave rise to the aspiration for the peerless, unequaled [Bodhi].
The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind comes to rest; this clarifies the expedient means for entering contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Next, Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage before the great assembly, and with his mind’s track perfectly luminous, a mixture of sorrow and joy, he inquired about the establishment of the site of practice (*maṇḍala*) and the methods for remaining far removed from demonic activities, desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future. This continues until the end of the section.
This ensures that whatever this person undertakes shall cease according to their wishes; this is the expedient means for gathering the mind.
These two expedient means generally belong to the practices cultivated by those at the initial stage of the path; therefore, they are called the "initial expedient means.

The twelve characters from the beginning of the seventh fascicle, which clarify the initial expedient means for the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* explained to Ānanda, have already been elucidated.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “We are dull-witted and fond of mere erudition;

regarding our minds of outflows, we had not yet sought liberation. Having received the compassionate instructions of the Buddha, we have attained correct cultivation, and our bodies and minds are tranquil, gaining great benefit.
World-Honored One, such is the cultivation and realization of the Buddha’s samādhi, though we have not yet reached nirvāṇa.”
What is called the stage of "Dry Wisdom" (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) involves the arising of forty-four mental states. This concludes the section from the eighth fascicle which states:

"One who performs this contemplation is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have false contemplation. This passage elucidates the eight characters concerning how the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained *bodhi*.
The general meaning therein is that delusion regarding the Truth results in the formation of the false, which are termed the twelve classes of living beings.
The cessation of delusion is called "True" and constitutes the twelve stages of the sages. First, the three gradual steps are clarified to demonstrate the practices that can be accomplished;
next, the fifty-five stages are clarified as the sacred positions that are thus accomplished; finally, it is concluded:

"In this manner, through the repeated layers of the single and the double [stages], the twelve are fully completed, and one reaches wondrous enlightenment to achieve the Unsurpassed Way. This "accomplishment" refers to the act of attaining accomplishment, and the "Unsurpassed Way" refers to...
This is Bodhi. Fearing that it might not be the Bodhi accomplished by the Tathāgatas, he again concludes:

"These various stages are all realized through pure cultivation and verification, using the ten profound metaphors of the diamond-like contemplation of illusion within *śamatha*, while employing the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas.
This corresponds to Ānanda’s request regarding the words "the Tathāgatas of the ten directions."

The elucidation of the meaning of the twenty characters concerning the initial expedient means for attaining the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is now complete. Ānanda’s request has been fully addressed;
his deep-seated delusions have been exhausted; and the Tathāgata’s body of awakening is perfected. Upon the path of correct cultivation, there remains no further doubt.
Therefore, as Mañjuśrī requested the name of this sutra, the Tathāgata established five titles for its definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
What has been revealed above constitutes the True Vehicle (*yāna*) of the complete power of the Way, which Ānanda requested;

it has not yet clarified the deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) of Ānanda’s regret over his incomplete power of the Way. After these words were spoken from within the eighth fascicle, immediately—Ānanda... [text continues]

The great assembly, having found it difficult to reach [this realization], was graced by the Tathāgata’s revelation of the meaning of the secret seal, the *Pañcarakṣā* (*Bhadrakarātrī*), as well as the hearing of the definitive titles of this sutra.
They suddenly awakened to the sublime principles for advancing through the stages of holy cultivation in *dhyāna*. From the beginning up to the end of the tenth fascicle, [the Buddha said]:
"You should take this root-source of deluded thought and cause your minds to attain penetration; transmit and reveal this to future generations during the Dharma-ending age."

Among these, the various practitioners are led to recognize the illusory nature [of existence], to develop a profound weariness with themselves, and to know that there is *nirvāṇa* such that they no longer cling to the three realms.

This precisely elucidates the meaning of the three phrases concerning Ānanda’s regret that, from time immemorial, he has been devoted solely to much-hearing (*bahuśruta*) without fully perfecting his power of the Way (*mārgabala*).
First, it clarifies that the emotions and perceptions of the seven destinies are the state of being deluded and not having fully perfected the power of the Way. Later, it clarifies the five...

The demons of the aggregates and the hindrances arise because one has not yet fully perfected the power of the Way within awakening; this means that both the paths of delusion and awakening have failed to clarify one’s own mind, as all are due to the power of the Way being incomplete.
As the Sutra says: "Within the true and eternal nature, one seeks for coming and going, delusion and awakening, or birth and death [and finds them not]."

It is utterly unattainable; this can be clearly seen herein. Thus one knows that the ten fascicles of this scripture, in both their words and meaning, do not exceed the nine phrases and thirty-six characters requested by Ānanda.
The subsequent section on the dissemination of the teaching consists merely of words of entrustment and praise.
When scholars read this scripture, they should be able to use these thirty-six characters to illuminate and penetrate the entire work.
According to this principle, the nature of the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses shall, in a single thought-moment, be transformed into supreme enlightened awareness.

Is this not a sudden transcendence beyond both delusion and awakening? Is this not a sudden clarification of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? Is this not a sudden realization of the pure, true reality (*dharmatā*)?
Upon reaching this point in the scripture, the mind and its objects are suddenly fused; subject and object both vanish, and the body, mind, and world become entirely the Great Buddha-Crown.
It is the King of Śūraṅgama Samādhi. Does it not possess great kindness, great compassion, great heroism, great power, and great liberation?
Those of like mind should devote their whole hearts to it.
A Suspended Discussion on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra (Conclusion)
